title: Run a Feature Decision Table Before Writing the Implementation
summary:
A feature can sound settled until someone asks about a specific combination of inputs.

An editor can share a document. Inactive members cannot share. What happens when an editor's membership is inactive?

That question can surface in a planning meeting, during implementation, or after release. Intent Workbench provides a small place to examine such cases before the rules are embedded in application code.

Make the disagreement executable

The inputs are explicit facts such as role, visibility, and membership status. The model is a bounded decision table supplied by the team. The evaluator shows which rules match and whether they resolve to a consistent outcome.

The important distinction is between a model that can be parsed and a model whose rules cover a particular case. A structurally valid table can contain conflicting behavior.

For the editor with inactive membership, the bundled v1 model matches rules that produce conflicting outcomes. The evaluator returns a conflict, with the relevant rule IDs and no chosen prediction. It does not use the order of the rules to conceal the disagreement.

Other outcomes need their own explanations. Missing input is different from a case where every required fact is present but no rule matches. A useful feature conversation should be able to distinguish those states.

Explore the conflict

Use Python 3.11 or newer. The CLI runtime uses only the standard library:

git clone https://github.com/asadani/intent-workbench.git
cd intent-workbench
out_dir="$(mktemp -d)"

python -m intent_workbench validate fixtures/sharing-v1.json

python -m intent_workbench evaluate fixtures/sharing-v1.json \
  --input fixtures/input.json --out "$out_dir/evaluation.json"

Validation succeeds. Evaluation exits with status 1, which is expected for the deliberately conflicting case. The resulting JSON has a conflict status, a null outcome, and the matching rules.

Next, compare the proposed revision against saved cases:

python -m intent_workbench compare \
  fixtures/sharing-v1.json fixtures/sharing-v2.json \
  fixtures/cases.json --out "$out_dir/comparison.json"

python -m intent_workbench build fixtures/sharing-v2.json \
  --out "$out_dir/workbench.html"

The comparison identifies the prediction change for the editor/inactive case. The HTML output is a self-contained workbench for adjusting input values and inspecting outcomes in a browser.

Keep expected behavior separate from predictions

A rule engine can tell you what a table predicts. It cannot tell you whether the product team intended that prediction.

Saved cases therefore distinguish human-confirmed expectations from model predictions. Exporting a case should not promote whichever result the evaluator happened to produce into an approved requirement.

This separation is especially useful when a revision changes several cases. A team can inspect each change, agree on the intended behavior, and retain that expectation for implementation work. A changed prediction is an invitation to discuss the requirement, not an automatic update to the acceptance criteria.

Use a deliberately small language

The current rules support equality, membership, integer bounds, and conjunction across a rule's conditions. They do not contain arbitrary expressions, priorities, prose extraction, or production enforcement.

That boundary keeps the table reviewable. It also means teams must supply the meaning of the inputs. If group inheritance determines membership, another system or discussion must establish that fact. The workbench does not implement the inheritance semantics itself.

The model is useful only if the people responsible for the feature can inspect and accept it. A large table no one understands would move the ambiguity into a different file.

Bring three awkward cases to planning

Start with one feature and a few combinations that could plausibly cause disagreement. Include a normal case, a boundary case, and a case where two rules appear to compete. Inspect the matching rules together before discussing code structure.

The test of value is whether this reveals unresolved decisions early and leaves reusable, confirmed cases. A deterministic answer is easy to produce; an agreed answer is the artifact worth keeping.

The MIT-licensed repository includes the two model revisions, case fixtures, CLI commands, and offline HTML builder.

title: I built SpecTerm – a fast, modern Bash terminal for Windows in pure Rust
summary:
I built SpecTerm because I wanted a fast, modern Linux-style Bash terminal on Windows without dealing with WSL overhead or heavy Electron apps.

It's written natively in Rust using Direct3D 11, DirectComposition, DirectWrite 5, alacritty_terminal, and Microsoft's OpenConsole ConPTY (~38 MB RAM, zero Electron or WebView2).

What's in v1.0

  • Linux-style Bash out of the box (bundled Git Bash, plus PowerShell, CMD, and WSL tabs)
  • Binary split panes and floating regex search (Ctrl+Shift+F)
  • Smart live resize (clean ls column reflow with zero prompt glitches)
  • Frosted-glass UI & 6 optional GPU minimize effects (including Liquid Genie tracking your taskbar icon)
  • Explorer right-click integration ("Open in SpecTerm")

Try it out

Free and MIT open source — available as both a Windows installer (SpecTerm-Setup.exe) and a zero-trace portable ZIP (SpecTerm-Portable.zip):

VECNA-cpp / SpecTerm

Super lightweight, blazing-fast Linux-style Bash terminal for Windows — pure native Rust, Direct3D 11 GPU glass, split panes, 6 minimize animations & zero Electron (~38 MB RAM).

Why SpecTerm?

Built to bring the fast, clean Linux Bash terminal experience straight to Windows—without heavy Electron/WebView2 wrappers burning hundreds of megabytes of RAM, and without fighting clunky default Windows consoles.

SpecTerm ships ready to run with a bundled Bash engine (authentic Linux/GNU ls, instant zero-fork prompt, persistent Bash history, plus optional PowerShell, CMD, and WSL tabs) powered by pure native Rust, Direct3D 11, DirectComposition, Direct2D, DirectWrite 5, alacritty_terminal, and Microsoft's modern OpenConsole ConPTY—staying super lightweight (~6 MB binary, ~38 MB RAM) with 60 FPS smoky glass and GPU polish.

title: Python 3.14 Free Threaded: Install, Benchmark and the Packages That Re-enable the GIL
summary:
Python 3.14 Free Threaded: Install, Benchmark and the Packages That Re-enable the GIL

Python 3.14 is the first release where the free-threaded build is officially supported, not experimental. This guide to Python 3.14 free threaded shows how to install it with uv, how to check that the GIL is really off, what scaling we measured on 8 cores, a race condition that only appears without the GIL, and which common packages still switch it back on.

Tested with CPython 3.14.10 (both the default and the 3.14t free-threaded builds) installed through uv 0.13.9, on an 8-core Linux x86-64 machine. The commands and outputs below are from that machine. We could not build a Docker image there, so the container section is based on the same uv commands plus the official image tag list.

What "free threaded" means in Python 3.14

A normal CPython build has a global interpreter lock (GIL): only one thread runs Python bytecode at a time, so CPU-bound threads do not speed up. The free-threaded build removes that lock. Threads run in parallel on separate cores, at the cost of a different ABI, extra memory use and a small single-thread slowdown.

The official Python docs describe it plainly: free-threaded execution allows full use of available processing power, "while not all software will benefit from this automatically", and some third-party packages with extension modules "will re-enable the GIL". On the pyperformance suite the docs put the average single-threaded overhead between about 1% on macOS aarch64 and 8% on x86-64 Linux.

It is a separate interpreter, not a flag on the normal one. The binary is called python3.14t. A wheel built for the normal interpreter (cp314) will not load there; it needs a cp314t build.

Install Python 3.14 free threaded with uv

uv knows the t suffix:

uv python install 3.14t
uv run --python 3.14t python -VV
uv venv --python 3.14t .venv

python -VV prints "free-threading build" in the version string. To check the GIL state in a running process, use the function the docs recommend:

import sys, sysconfig
print(sysconfig.get_config_var("Py_GIL_DISABLED"))  # 1 on a free-threaded build
print(sys._is_gil_enabled())                         # False when the GIL is off

The two answers differ on purpose. The config variable tells you what the build can do. sys._is_gil_enabled() tells you what the process is doing right now. On our box:

3.14.10  Py_GIL_DISABLED = 0  gil enabled = True     (default build)
3.14.10  Py_GIL_DISABLED = 1  gil enabled = False    (3.14t)
3.14.10  Py_GIL_DISABLED = 1  gil enabled = True     (3.14t with PYTHON_GIL=1)

You can force the lock back on with the PYTHON_GIL=1 environment variable or -X gil=1, and off with 0. We confirmed python -X gil=1 reports the GIL as enabled.

Python 3.14 free threaded benchmark

The test is deliberately simple: a recursive fib(32) in N threads, with N from 1 to 4, timed with time.perf_counter().

import threading, time

def fib(n):
    return n if n < 2 else fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)

def run(nthreads, n=32):
    ts = [threading.Thread(target=fib, args=(n,)) for _ in range(nthreads)]
    start = time.perf_counter()
    for t in ts: t.start()
    for t in ts: t.join()
    return time.perf_counter() - start

Results (the free-threaded numbers are from two runs, which agreed within noise):

Build 1 thread 2 threads 4 threads Throughput vs serial at 4 threads
3.14 (GIL) 0.15 s 0.30 s 0.60 s 1.0x
3.14t (GIL off) 0.15 s 0.15 s 0.15 to 0.16 s 3.6x to 3.9x
3.14t, PYTHON_GIL=1 0.15 s 0.30 s 0.62 s 1.0x

Four threads on the normal build take four times as long as one, because they queue on the lock. On 3.14t they all finish in about the time of one. Setting PYTHON_GIL=1 on the free-threaded interpreter brought the old behaviour straight back, which is a handy way to A/B test your own code.

Single-thread speed was the same to two decimal places in this one benchmark. Do not read that as "no overhead": the docs' 1% to 8% average is across many workloads, and a different benchmark will show a gap.

Not everything scales

We also ran a thread pool hashing 8 buffers with hashlib.sha256 (300,000 rounds each, 64-byte inputs):

title: CSV Clean X: Robust Python CSV Pipelines
summary:
CSV Clean X: A Robust Python Library for CSV Pipelines

When working with data pipelines in Python, cleaning and standardizing CSV data is a common bottleneck. Today, we're introducing CSV Clean X, a lightweight and robust Python library designed to streamline data cleaning, whitespace stripping, missing value handling, and duplicate removal.

Features

  • Whitespace Stripping: Automatically cleans leading and trailing whitespaces from string fields.
  • Missing Value Handling: Option to drop rows with missing or empty values.
  • Duplicate Removal: Ensures unique dataset rows effortlessly.
  • Lightweight & Fast: Zero heavy dependencies, pure Python implementation with robust unit testing.

Installation & Usage

You can find the project repository on GitHub: qtnt2xxx-wq/csv-clean-x.

from csv_clean_x.pipeline import CsvCleanPipeline

data = [
    {"name": " Alice ", "age": "30"},
    {"name": "Bob", "age": "25"},
    {"name": " Alice ", "age": "30"}
]

pipeline = CsvCleanPipeline(data)
cleaned_data = pipeline.run(strip=True, drop_missing=False)
print(cleaned_data)

Check out the repo and contribute!

title: I Built a Memory That Learns From Failure. Then I Couldn't Find a Failure to Feed It.
summary:
A few weeks ago I wrote a post here arguing that my cheap models weren't dumb, they were missing a world model. It was 90% hypothesis and 10% hope. I had read about a third of a paper and built nothing.

This is the report from actually building it.

It does not end with a benchmark. It ends with two memory systems, one week of work I walked out of early, and a measurement problem I didn't see coming.

The setup, quickly

I build Mocu, an open-source, local-first desktop AI colleague. You bring your own OpenAI-compatible endpoint, which means I spend most of my time running it on cheap models, because that's the whole point of the thing.

And cheap models repeat themselves.

They try the same failing command twice. They read a wrong path, notice the path was wrong, and then read the wrong path again five minutes later with total confidence. Every tool I used before this explained the mistake to me beautifully, in detail, afterwards. Thanks. I already knew it broke.

What I wanted was the opposite: tell the model no, don't do that before the command runs. Not a post-mortem. A prediction.

The paper that gave me a shape for this is Self-Evolving World Models for LLM Agent Planning (EMNLP 2026 Findings). The short version: keep the agent frozen, and let a world model improve by evolving its context instead of its weights. Episodic memory of real action→outcome transitions, semantic memory that turns a bad prediction into a written rule, and a confidence filter that drops predictions the system doesn't believe.

No gradients. No training run. The improvement lives in text files.

That last part is why it fit my constraints at all. Mocu is Apache 2.0 and everything lives in local files you can read and edit. There's no server collecting traces and no pipeline to rent. Text is the only kind of learning I can actually ship.

Day one and two: I built a pipe

Day one went into finishing the paper. No code.

Day two I built exactly one thing: I routed every tool call the agent makes through the world-model code. Now the system physically sits between the agent and its tools. The agent cannot act without passing through it.

That felt great for about ten minutes.

Then I realized I had built a pipe and had no idea what was supposed to flow through it. How does a prediction get made? How does the agent even understand one when it arrives? Is it a warning, a rewritten plan, a blocked call? I had no answer, and the paper didn't hand me one I could wire into a real running system.

So I did what I usually do: left the question open and built the part I could build.

Day three: the "simple" one

Episodic memory. Store what the agent did, read it back, warn before it repeats a failure. In the paper this is half a page. It looked trivial.

It took a full day and forced me to reverse two things I felt strongly about.

One: where the data lives. Mocu already keeps every tool call in the project folder. My instinct was not to duplicate it. I tested that and it didn't hold. It had to go into the global folder as well.

Two: how much to store. I did not want to write every single tool call into a memory database. It felt wasteful and messy.

I now write every single tool call into it.

Both decisions came out against my instinct and I'm still not sure either one is final. "Simple" should come with a health warning.

The mechanism, plainly:

  1. Every tool call gets stored with its outcome.
  2. Before an action, a BM25 search pulls the closest past calls, and a small decision model picks the one that's genuinely closest.
  3. The system checks how that past call turned out.
  4. If it worked: silence, nothing happens.
  5. If it failed: the model gets one line. This is very close to something that failed before.

Before, not after. That's the entire feature.

And then it worked better than I expected. Noticeably better. Fewer repeated mistakes, in early tests the difference wasn't subtle.

Which should have been the happy ending, and instead gave me a small alarm. Everything I know about this project says the real world ruins your nice plan. Here, the piece I thought would eat half a day behaved better than the paper promised and better than I designed it to. So something underneath might be wrong and just hasn't shown up yet.

I went into the next day more worried than I was before the win.

Day four: the tired one

Semantic memory is the part that was supposed to do the actual thinking.

The theory: a tool fails. First question, was it that tool's fault? A bad command, a wrong path, a malformed argument? Then it belongs to episodic memory and it's already handled. If not, the real cause is further back. So you walk backwards through the earlier calls, find the tool that actually caused the failure, and turn that into a warning so the agent doesn't repeat it.

The tool that fails is often not the tool that caused it. That's the whole reason this layer needs to exist.

That was the plan. It is not what I built.

I started that day exhausted. The hardest piece of the system, and I was running on empty. So I did the thing this project keeps making possible and probably shouldn't: I let Mocu write a large part of it.

The code runs. It exists. I don't trust it, because I didn't write most of it and I haven't reviewed it properly. My honest note to myself that evening was one sentence: I don't think it turned out well.

It also diverged from the paper. The paper's version is about cause and effect, actual reasoning about how one step produced the next outcome. That didn't make it in. What made it in is a much lighter mechanism that borrowed the name and very little else.

The paper called it semantic memory. So I call it semantic memory. The name stuck. The idea didn't.

Then the test, and the joke

I built the two memories in the wrong order, and that turned out to be a trap.

In the entire test session, there was exactly one failure that the second system could legitimately catch and fix.

One.

Everything else was either already caught by episodic memory or wasn't in semantic memory's category at all. The first memory guarded the door so well that the second one never got a customer.

No bug to fix. No proof of success either. Not broken, not proven. Just unmeasured.

Why I stopped at one week

I could keep going. I could write scenarios designed specifically to feed the second memory.

But the entire premise is that it learns from real mistakes, from real work, not incidents I invented to make my own test look good. Which means the honest test isn't a test. It's weeks of using Mocu normally, waiting for enough real failures to pile up that the system has something to study.

Weeks, not days. And I don't have weeks for this right now.

So the build is finished. Not because it's proven, but because it's finished. I'm walking away and letting reality do the testing. That's how it ended: one week out of the two I gave myself, two memories, one visibly working, one I can't see yet.

The actual lesson, which isn't about memory

I spent a week building something whose entire job is to prevent mistakes, and found out that prevention is a terrible thing to measure.

Every mistake it stops is a mistake that never appears in your logs. So you end up trusting a system based on the absence of evidence, which is the exact thing you're told never to do.

Three times in this project reality argued with my plan. I thought the architecture would be easy and the magic would be hard. It was backwards. I thought the simple memory would take half a day. It took the whole day. I thought a working memory would prove itself. It didn't. It just made the second one invisible.

Maybe that's the real shape of self-improving systems. Not a moment where it gets smart. Just a slow pile of mistakes that stop happening.

What's next, and what I want to know

Two failure modes are on my short list and both are embarrassing:

  • Self-confirming memory. If the agent retrieves its own past predictions instead of past outcomes, it will happily agree with itself forever. The store has to be outcomes only.
  • Rules that breed superstition. Enough one-off heuristics and your context window becomes a collection of coincidences. Requiring a pattern to recur before promoting it is probably the fix, and it means the system learns slower, maybe not at all in a session.

If you've built something in this direction (externalized prediction, memory that writes its own rules, agents that are allowed to say "no idea"), I'd like to hear what broke. Especially the part where the memory poisoned itself.

event_model_payload.headline: I Built a Memory That Learns From Failure. Then I Couldn't Find a Failure to Feed It.
event_model_payload.summary:
A few weeks ago I wrote a post here arguing that my cheap models weren't dumb, they were missing a world model. It was 90% hypothesis and 10% hope. I had read about a third of a paper and built nothing.

This is the report from actually building it.

It does not end with a benchmark. It ends with two memory systems, one week of work I walked out of early, and a measurement problem I didn't see coming.

The setup, quickly

I build Mocu, an open-source, local-first desktop AI colleague. You bring your own OpenAI-compatible endpoint, which means I spend most of my time running it on cheap models, because that's the whole point of the thing.

And cheap models repeat themselves.

They try the same failing command twice. They read a wrong path, notice the path was wrong, and then read the wrong path again five minutes later with total confidence. Every tool I used before this explained the mistake to me beautifully, in detail, afterwards. Thanks. I already knew it broke.

What I wanted was the opposite: tell the model no, don't do that before the command runs. Not a post-mortem. A prediction.

The paper that gave me a shape for this is Self-Evolving World Models for LLM Agent Planning (EMNLP 2026 Findings). The short version: keep the agent frozen, and let a world model improve by evolving its context instead of its weights. Episodic memory of real action→outcome transitions, semantic memory that turns a bad prediction into a written rule, and a confidence filter that drops predictions the system doesn't believe.

No gradients. No training run. The improvement lives in text files.

That last part is why it fit my constraints at all. Mocu is Apache 2.0 and everything lives in local files you can read and edit. There's no server collecting traces and no pipeline to rent. Text is the only kind of learning I can actually ship.

Day one and two: I built a pipe

Day one went into finishing the paper. No code.

Day two I built exactly one thing: I routed every tool call the agent makes through the world-model code. Now the system physically sits between the agent and its tools. The agent cannot act without passing through it.

That felt great for about ten minutes.

Then I realized I had built a pipe and had no idea what was supposed to flow through it. How does a prediction get made? How does the agent even understand one when it arrives? Is it a warning, a rewritten plan, a blocked call? I had no answer, and the paper didn't hand me one I could wire into a real running system.

So I did what I usually do: left the question open and built the part I could build.

Day three: the "simple" one

Episodic memory. Store what the agent did, read it back, warn before it repeats a failure. In the paper this is half a page. It looked trivial.

It took a full day and forced me to reverse two things I felt strongly about.

One: where the data lives. Mocu already keeps every tool call in the project folder. My instinct was not to duplicate it. I tested that and it didn't hold. It had to go into the global folder as well.

Two: how much to store. I did not want to write every single tool call into a memory database. It felt wasteful and messy.

I now write every single tool call into it.

Both decisions came out against my instinct and I'm still not sure either one is final. "Simple" should come with a health warning.

The mechanism, plainly:

  1. Every tool call gets stored with its outcome.
  2. Before an action, a BM25 search pulls the closest past calls, and a small decision model picks the one that's genuinely closest.
  3. The system checks how that past call turned out.
  4. If it worked: silence, nothing happens.
  5. If it failed: the model gets one line. This is very close to something that failed before.

Before, not after. That's the entire feature.

And then it worked better than I expected. Noticeably better. Fewer repeated mistakes, in early tests the difference wasn't subtle.

Which should have been the happy ending, and instead gave me a small alarm. Everything I know about this project says the real world ruins your nice plan. Here, the piece I thought would eat half a day behaved better than the paper promised and better than I designed it to. So something underneath might be wrong and just hasn't shown up yet.

I went into the next day more worried than I was before the win.

Day four: the tired one

Semantic memory is the part that was supposed to do the actual thinking.

The theory: a tool fails. First question, was it that tool's fault? A bad command, a wrong path, a malformed argument? Then it belongs to episodic memory and it's already handled. If not, the real cause is further back. So you walk backwards through the earlier calls, find the tool that actually caused the failure, and turn that into a warning so the agent doesn't repeat it.

The tool that fails is often not the tool that caused it. That's the whole reason this layer needs to exist.

That was the plan. It is not what I built.

I started that day exhausted. The hardest piece of the system, and I was running on empty. So I did the thing this project keeps making possible and probably shouldn't: I let Mocu write a large part of it.

The code runs. It exists. I don't trust it, because I didn't write most of it and I haven't reviewed it properly. My honest note to myself that evening was one sentence: I don't think it turned out well.

It also diverged from the paper. The paper's version is about cause and effect, actual reasoning about how one step produced the next outcome. That didn't make it in. What made it in is a much lighter mechanism that borrowed the name and very little else.

The paper called it semantic memory. So I call it semantic memory. The name stuck. The idea didn't.

Then the test, and the joke

I built the two memories in the wrong order, and that turned out to be a trap.

In the entire test session, there was exactly one failure that the second system could legitimately catch and fix.

One.

Everything else was either already caught by episodic memory or wasn't in semantic memory's category at all. The first memory guarded the door so well that the second one never got a customer.

No bug to fix. No proof of success either. Not broken, not proven. Just unmeasured.

Why I stopped at one week

I could keep going. I could write scenarios designed specifically to feed the second memory.

But the entire premise is that it learns from real mistakes, from real work, not incidents I invented to make my own test look good. Which means the honest test isn't a test. It's weeks of using Mocu normally, waiting for enough real failures to pile up that the system has something to study.

Weeks, not days. And I don't have weeks for this right now.

So the build is finished. Not because it's proven, but because it's finished. I'm walking away and letting reality do the testing. That's how it ended: one week out of the two I gave myself, two memories, one visibly working, one I can't see yet.

The actual lesson, which isn't about memory

I spent a week building something whose entire job is to prevent mistakes, and found out that prevention is a terrible thing to measure.

Every mistake it stops is a mistake that never appears in your logs. So you end up trusting a system based on the absence of evidence, which is the exact thing you're told never to do.

Three times in this project reality argued with my plan. I thought the architecture would be easy and the magic would be hard. It was backwards. I thought the simple memory would take half a day. It took the whole day. I thought a working memory would prove itself. It didn't. It just made the second one invisible.

Maybe that's the real shape of self-improving systems. Not a moment where it gets smart. Just a slow pile of mistakes that stop happening.

What's next, and what I want to know

Two failure modes are on my short list and both are embarrassing:

  • Self-confirming memory. If the agent retrieves its own past predictions instead of past outcomes, it will happily agree with itself forever. The store has to be outcomes only.
  • Rules that breed superstition. Enough one-off heuristics and your context window becomes a collection of coincidences. Requiring a pattern to recur before promoting it is probably the fix, and it means the system learns slower, maybe not at all in a session.

title: Building a Lightweight Vietnamese Lo Ban Ruler Calculator with Vanilla JS
summary:
In Vietnamese architecture and interior design, the Lo Ban Ruler (Thước Lỗ Ban) is commonly used to check auspicious dimensions for doors, furniture, and home layouts. Instead of relying on heavy frameworks or external APIs, you can model all three standard Lo Ban rulers in just a few lines of Vanilla JavaScript using modulo arithmetic and lookup arrays.

Understanding the Three Ruler Cycles

Each Lo Ban ruler repeats periodically along a fixed length, divided into major segments (cung lớn) and minor sub-segments (cung nhỏ):

  1. 52.2 cm (Thông Thủy) — Used for clear openings such as doors, windows, and hallways (8 major segments of 6.525 cm, each split into 5 sub-segments).
  2. 42.9 cm (Dương Trạch) — Used for solid structures and furniture like desks, beds, and cabinets (8 major segments, 4 sub-segments each).
  3. 38.8 cm (Âm Phần) — Used for altars and memorial dimensions (10 major segments of 3.88 cm, 4 sub-segments each).

Core Modulo Calculation in JavaScript

To evaluate any input measurement mm against a ruler cycle cycleMm and an ordered array of segment definitions:

function checkLoBan(lengthMm, cycleMm, segments) {
  if (lengthMm <= 0) return null;
  // Normalize measurement into a single ruler cycle
  const posInCycle = ((lengthMm % cycleMm) + cycleMm) % cycleMm;
  const segmentSize = cycleMm / segments.length;
  const index = Math.min(
    Math.floor(posInCycle / segmentSize),
    segments.length - 1
  );
  return {
    positionMm: Number(posInCycle.toFixed(2)),
    segment: segments[index],
  };
}

By keeping the ruler definitions as pure JSON/array data and computing positions client-side in mm, the UI stays instantaneous even when dragging a virtual ruler slider in real time.

Live Demo & Source Code

We built an open-source, zero-dependency online lookup tool combining all three rulers (52.2cm, 42.9cm, 38.8cm) with instant search and visual scale rendering:

  • Live Demo: Tra cứu Thước Lỗ Ban Online
  • Source Code (GitHub): lequy240193/thuoc-lo-ban-phong-thuy
  • Project Homepage: Phong Thủy Thức Tâm

Feedback and pull requests for improving accessibility or adding SVG ruler rendering are always welcome!

title: Introducing RepoLens: Looking Beyond the Code 🔍
summary:
A small project, a lot of learning, and my first public release.

I've always been interested in building tools that solve practical problems for developers.

So, I decided to build something of my own: RepoLens.

RepoLens is a lightweight, cross-platform repository analysis tool built with Python. It scans a project directory, analyses its source files, and generates a report with statistics and an overall score.

GitHub Repository: https://github.com/AdityaTyagi-Dev/RepoLens

Why did I build RepoLens?

When working with code, we often focus on whether the program works.

But there's more to a project than just working code.

How readable is it?

Are the lines unnecessarily long?

Does the project have proper documentation?

I wanted to explore these questions by building a tool that could analyse a repository and present some useful insights.

That became RepoLens.

What can RepoLens do?

The initial release, v0.1.0-alpha, focuses on three analysis metrics:

1. Comment Density

Analyses the relationship between comment lines and code lines to provide an overview of code commenting.

2. Long Line Analysis

Identifies unnecessarily long lines in source files and calculates their proportion.

3. README Analysis

Checks the project's README file and analyses basic information such as its presence, size, word count and character count.

These metrics contribute to an overall score out of 100.

The scoring system currently uses heuristic thresholds, so the score is an initial indicator rather than a definitive measure of code quality.

How is it structured?

One of the things I focused on was keeping responsibilities separate.

The current architecture follows three important principles:

  • Scanner: Discovers directories and files.
  • Analyser: Decides what to analyse and performs the analysis.
  • Reporter: Presents the results in the terminal.

The rating engine handles score calculation separately.

I wanted each module to have a clear responsibility instead of putting everything into one large Python file.

Technologies used

  • Python
  • pathlib
  • Python Standard Library

One thing I'm happy about is that RepoLens currently requires no external Python dependencies.

What's next?

This is only the initial release.

There are plenty of things I'd like to explore in future versions, including:

  • More repository analysis metrics
  • Improved language support
  • Better code-quality analysis
  • Project structure analysis
  • Documentation and testing analysis

I want to improve RepoLens gradually while keeping its architecture maintainable.

What I learned

Building RepoLens taught me more than just writing Python code.

I got to work on file-system traversal, language identification, modular architecture, analysis logic, scoring systems, error handling, and packaging a project for a public release.

Most importantly, I experienced the process of taking an idea, turning it into a working project, and publishing it on GitHub.

Try RepoLens

The project is open source, and I'd genuinely appreciate feedback, suggestions, and contributions.

🔗 GitHub: https://github.com/AdityaTyagi-Dev/RepoLens

This is my first public release, and I'm looking forward to improving it.

Build. Learn. Improve. Repeat.

I'm a student developer at NIT Patna, exploring software development, Python, AI, and open source through hands-on projects.

title: Ant's 6B Ming-Image-0.2-Design Tops the Open-Weight Image Chart — With One Catch
summary:
Ant Group's InclusionAI team quietly shipped one of the most interesting open model releases of the month: Ming-Image-0.2-Design, a 6-billion-parameter text-to-image model built specifically for visual design work. The weights are on Hugging Face under an MIT license, and as of November 25 it sits first among open-weight models on Artificial Analysis' text-to-image leaderboard (AA-Image-T2I v2.1), at 1,095 Elo.

That headline deserves a closer look — both because the model is genuinely useful, and because the fine print matters more than the ranking.

What it actually is

Ming-Image-0.2-Design is not a general-purpose image generator trying to beat the closed frontier models at everything. It is a design-specialized model, and the model card is explicit about the target: e-commerce hero images, UI design drafts, and spatial renderings, with an emphasis on complex composition, lighting, and legible text.

That specialization is the whole point. General image models are good at "a cat in a spacesuit." Design work is harder: a landing page hero with a headline, a subheading, a button, and three feature cards — all spelled correctly, all in the right place, all in a consistent style. Text rendering and layout discipline are where most open models fall apart, and they are exactly what this release targets.

The model is a 6B diffusion transformer (DiT). It ships with a prompt enhancer, and the team recommends Figma-style structured prompts — layers listed back to front, every string of text quoted exactly once — over plain prose. It also pairs with Ling-3.2-flash to turn a design concept into an interactive page, and the companion repo includes agent workflows for UI design and for recreating a generated page or slide image as an editable PowerPoint file.

The leaderboard number, honestly

Artificial Analysis lists Ming-Image-0.2-Design at 1,095 Elo from 4,936 human preference votes, ranked 24th overall and first among open-weight models. It is the only open-weight model in the top 25.

Two things worth knowing before you quote that number:

  • The lead is narrow. The 95% confidence interval is 1,083 to 1,107. That is a real first place, not a rounding error — but it is not a blowout, and a few hundred more votes could shuffle the order.
  • Rank 24 overall is the honest frame. Twenty-three closed models still sit above it. "Best open model" is a meaningful title, but it is not "best model." If you need the absolute best image quality and do not care about self-hosting, the closed APIs are still ahead.

What the ranking does prove is narrower and more useful: for design-flavored generation, an open model you can run yourself is now competitive with the hosted options most teams actually pay for.

What it costs to run

This is where the story gets practical. The validated setup is one CUDA GPU with 80 GiB of VRAM, running in BF16, with 12 sampling steps, a CFG scale of 1.0, and 2048×2048 output by default (1024×1024 for faster drafts). The repo provides vLLM-Omni recipes for serving.

That is a serious GPU — an H100 or equivalent — but it is also a single GPU, not a cluster. For a studio or an e-commerce team generating product visuals all day, one card that you own beats a per-image API bill, and the MIT license means you can use the outputs commercially, modify the weights, and redistribute without extra paperwork. Compare that with FLUX.1 [dev], which ships under non-commercial terms: the license, as much as the Elo score, is the reason to care.

The quick start is refreshingly short:

git clone https://github.com/inclusionAI/Ming-Image
cd Ming-Image
pip install -r requirements.txt

python infer.py \
  --model inclusionAI/Ming-Image-0.2-Design \
  --task text-to-image \
  --prompt "Landing page for a productivity app called Flow. Clean minimal design, white background, generous whitespace." \
  --width 2048 --height 2048 \
  --output-dir outputs/flow

One gap: there is no hosted per-image price yet. Artificial Analysis lists the hosted price as "coming soon," and the model is not on OpenRouter or other aggregators. For now this is a self-hosting story. If you do not have an 80 GiB GPU, you wait.

The catch: the layer trick is not in this download

The flashiest part of the launch demos is layer decomposition: the model splits a finished design into transparent, independently editable layers — in one demo, a character separated into 35 sublayers for motion design. That is the feature that would change a designer's workflow, because it turns a flat image into something you can actually edit.

Here is the catch: that layer model is not part of today's release. The repository's layer-decomposition inference still runs on the previous 0.1 layer model, and Ant says the upgraded 0.2 layer model follows next week. The model card describes the refined decomposition — down to character parts — as part of the upgrade, but the downloadable piece that does it is the older one.

So do not plan a workflow around layer editing yet. What you get today is the generator: strong composition, clean text, and a design-first prompt format. The editable-layers part is a preview, and it is worth waiting to see whether the shipped version matches the demo.

Who should care

  • E-commerce and marketing teams generating hero images and product visuals at volume, on their own hardware, under a license that allows commercial use.
  • Design tool builders who want a model that understands layout and text instead of treating every prompt like a photo caption.
  • Anyone self-hosting image generation who has been waiting for an open model that is actually good at the boring, commercial work — not just the impressive demo images.

And who should wait: anyone without a big GPU, anyone who needs editable layers today, and anyone who just wants the highest-quality single image — the closed models still win that comparison.

Bottom line

Ming-Image-0.2-Design is a genuinely useful release, and its most important number is not the Elo score. It is the combination of three facts: first among open-weight models, MIT licensed, and runnable on a single GPU. That is a package no other image model currently offers for design work.

Just do not mistake the demos for the download. The generator is here and worth trying. The layer editor — the part that would actually change how designers work — is still on its way.

Sources: the Ming-Image-0.2-Design model card on Hugging Face, the Ming-Image repository on GitHub, and the Artificial Analysis text-to-image leaderboard.

So do not plan a workflow around layer editing yet. What you get today is the generator: strong composition, clean text, and a design-first prompt format. The editable-layers part is a preview, and it is worth waiting to see whether the shipped version matches the demo.

Who should care

  • E-commerce and marketing teams generating hero images and product visuals at volume, on their own hardware, under a license that allows commercial use.
  • Design tool builders who want a model that understands layout and text instead of treating every prompt like a photo caption.
  • Anyone self-hosting image generation who has been waiting for an open model that is actually good at the boring, commercial work — not just the impressive demo images.

And who should wait: anyone without a big GPU, anyone who needs editable layers today, and anyone who just wants the highest-quality single image — the closed models still win that comparison.

Bottom line

Ming-Image-0.2-Design is a genuinely useful release, and its most important number is not the Elo score. It is the combination of three facts: first among open-weight models, MIT licensed, and runnable on a single GPU. That is a package no other image model currently offers for design work.

Just do not mistake the demos for the download. The generator is here and worth trying. The layer editor — the part that would actually change how designers work — is still on its way.

title: Python (13.31) vs TypeScript (2.36) vs Rust (1.71) vs Go (1.40): Supply-Chain Review Risk Across 3,620 GitHub Repos
summary:
There is nothing inherently wrong with generating code using AI coding assistants. Most engineering teams rely on LLMs daily for scaffolding, refactors, and test generation.

The real architectural bottleneck is review throughput versus generation velocity - specifically how different language ecosystems absorb unverified dependencies, dynamic import patterns, and silent failure wrappers when pull request volume scales up.

While maintaining the SlopCodeMonitor empirical observatory (7,135 open-source repositories, ~3.8B lines of code), one cross-language divergence stood out sharply in the static supply-chain heuristic indices.

Cross-Language Supply-Chain Review Index (0-100 Heuristic Scale)

Across uniform schema and scoring versions (1.0.0 / 2.0.0 / heuristic-density-v1), here is how six major ecosystems compare on static dependency and supply-chain review prompts:

Ecosystem Scanned Repositories Mean Supply-Chain Index (/100) Cohort Benchmark Page

TypeScript 1,219 2.36 TypeScript Supply-Chain Benchmark

Java 304 1.95 Java Supply-Chain Benchmark
Rust 483 1.71 Rust Supply-Chain Benchmark
Go 659 1.40 Go Supply-Chain Benchmark

(Full 121-language distribution available in the Supply-Chain Pattern Signals by Language matrix.)

Methodology caveat: These scores are deterministic static heuristics meant to prioritize human code review and dependency verification - not proof of AI authorship and not confirmed malicious or hallucinated package incidents.

Why Python Scores ~8x Higher Than Rust and Go

Three structural properties explain why Python repositories surface dramatically higher static dependency-review density than Go (1.40) or Rust (1.71):

  1. Runtime Import Resolution vs Compile-Time Module Graphs: In Rust (Cargo.lock + rustc) and Go (go.sum + explicit module paths), unresolved or undeclared transitive imports fail compilation immediately. In Python, optional imports nested inside try / except ImportError: branches, importlib.import_module() calls, and plugin registries routinely defer resolution to runtime.
  2. Rapid AI Agent & Glue-Code Concentration: Python hosts the overwhelming majority of newly created LLM orchestration, RAG, and skill-wrapper repositories, where contributors frequently copy multi-provider SDK snippets without pruning unused imports or pinning transitive hashes.
  3. Namespace vs Package-Name Mismatches: PyPI distribution names (scikit-learn, pillow, pyyaml, beautifulsoup4) frequently differ from top-level import identifiers (sklearn, PIL, yaml, bs4), creating fertile ground for slopsquatting when coding assistants hallucinate plausible package names in requirements.txt.

  • On TypeScript / Node: Audit postinstall scripts (--ignore-scripts in CI where feasible) and flag dynamic require() / import() expressions.
  • On Go & Rust: Focus reviewer budget less on phantom imports and more on cognitive ownership (unsafe blocks in Rust, goroutine lifecycle and context cancellation in Go).

title: Is Self-Hosted Hubs Worth It? Open Source Alternative to VRChat and Horizon Worlds for Private Family Meetups
summary:
Yes, for families and small groups who mainly want privacy and can live with simpler worlds than VRChat or Meta Horizon Worlds. A self-hosted Hubs server runs in the browser, lets guests join from a link without creating a platform account, and keeps voice, chat and room data on infrastructure you choose. The cost is running a real server stack yourself, and accepting fewer worlds and fewer people online than on the big commercial platforms.

TL;DR:

  • Parents hosting a remote family gathering (grandparents on laptops, teenagers on a Quest): self-host Hubs, because nobody needs a Meta or VRChat account and the room exists only on your server.
  • A teacher running a small private class or club: Hubs is a strong fit, because link-based access and room permissions suit a closed group better than a public social platform.
  • A friend group that wants games, avatars and huge user-made worlds: stay on VRChat, because Hubs has nothing like its content library and community.
  • Someone already inside the Meta ecosystem who only meets other Quest owners: Horizon Worlds is the lower-effort choice, provided you accept Meta's data policies.
  • A privacy-focused small organisation (a nonprofit board, a support group): self-host Hubs, because accounts, logs and retention stay under your own policy instead of a vendor's.
  • A non-technical user with no help available: use a managed hosting option or wait, because the Hubs server stack is more involved than a typical one-container app.

The central tradeoff: with Hubs you exchange the content, polish and scale of commercial social VR for control over who sees your voices, faces and identities.

Table of contents

  • What does Hubs actually do, and how is it different from VRChat and Horizon Worlds?
  • Who maintains Hubs now that Mozilla no longer runs it?
  • Do your guests need an account to join a Hubs room?
  • Where does your voice go during a virtual meetup?
  • Account and identity data compared across Hubs, VRChat and Horizon Worlds
  • What can a social VR platform track about you beyond voice?
  • Is Hubs a safe choice for children and family gatherings?
  • Room permissions and moderation tools for small private groups
  • Which headsets, laptops and phones can join a Hubs room?
  • What does self-hosting Hubs involve if you are not a sysadmin?
  • How much does a private Hubs server cost for a small group over 3 years?

What does Hubs actually do, and how is it different from VRChat and Horizon Worlds?

Hubs is open source software for shared 3D rooms that run in a web browser. You open a link, pick an avatar, and you are in a space where people talk using spatial audio: voices get louder as someone's avatar comes closer. You can share screens, drop in images, PDFs and 3D models, and move around with a mouse, a touchscreen or a VR headset. The code is published under the Mozilla Public License 2.0, so anyone can run their own server.

VRChat and Meta Horizon Worlds also offer shared rooms with avatars and voice, but they are built differently. Each one is a single commercial service run by one company, joined through that company's app and that company's account. Hubs is a piece of software you or a host of your choice can run, and every server is separate from the others.

Aspect Self-hosted Hubs VRChat and Horizon Worlds
How you join A room URL in any WebXR-capable browser A dedicated app on PC, headset or phone
Account Optional for guests, set by whoever runs the server Required: a VRChat account, or a Meta account for Horizon
Who runs it You, or a host you choose VRChat Inc. or Meta
Source code Open, MPL 2.0 Closed
World library Scenes you build in the Spoke editor or import Huge catalogues made by their user communities
Typical use Small private gatherings, classes, meetings Public social spaces, games, events

In practice this makes Hubs a private meeting room, not a social network. Discovery, friends lists and a big public community are missing on purpose, and you get to say who comes in.

Who maintains Hubs now that Mozilla no longer runs it?

Mozilla built Hubs and ran the public hubs.mozilla.com service for years. In February 2024 it announced it would stop, and it shut its servers down on 31 May 2024. Rooms hosted there disappeared unless their owners had exported them. The code survived because it was open source. Stewardship then went to the Hubs Foundation, a community nonprofit that maintains the repositories, documentation and community channels.

This history matters for privacy. A public service run by one organisation can close, change owner or change policy. A copy you host keeps working for as long as you keep the server running. The flip side is that there is no longer a big corporate team behind the code, so release cadence and support depend on volunteers and on the foundation's funding.

Today the main way to run your own server is Hubs Community Edition, which packages the stack (the Reticulum backend, the Dialog voice server, the web client and the Spoke editor) for container platforms. The official route targets Kubernetes. Mozilla's older AWS-based Hubs Cloud is deprecated. Where that stack can live:

  • A self-managed VPS: full control and the most flexibility, but you own Kubernetes, DNS, TLS and updates.
  • A home server: your data stays in your house, but home upload bandwidth limits how many voices and avatars you can serve.
  • A NAS: workable only on higher-end models with enough RAM, since Hubs is several services, not one container.
  • A managed personal cloud: Yundera is a managed Personal Cloud Server, built on CasaOS, that runs self-hosted apps as Docker containers on a server dedicated to the user. Check whether a given app store packages Hubs before you plan around it.

Do your guests need an account to join a Hubs room?

No, not by default. On a typical Hubs server a guest opens the room link, types a display name, picks an avatar, allows microphone access and walks in. The server never learns their email address, phone number or legal name. Compare VRChat, which needs a VRChat account before anyone enters a world and requires users to be at least 13, and Horizon Worlds, which ties every visitor to a Meta account.

When accounts are enabled, Hubs keeps them minimal. Signing in uses a one-time link sent by email, with no password stored on the server. The person running the server decides how much identity is needed:

  • Anonymous guests: anyone holding the room link can join under any display name. This collects the least data, but a forwarded link works for strangers too.
  • Signed-in users only: whoever runs the server can require an email sign-in before entry. You get accountability, and you now store an email address for each visitor.
  • Invite-only rooms: a room owner can switch access from a shared link to invitations, and revoke an invite link if it leaks. This suits recurring family or class meetings.
  • Room creation limits: the admin panel can stop anyone except admins from creating rooms, so visitors cannot use your server for their own events.
  • Single sign-on: some deployments put an external identity provider in front of Hubs. That adds another party who can see each login, so only use it if your group already trusts that provider.

The privacy-friendly default for a small group is anonymous entry to an invite-only room. Each person you invite discloses nothing beyond a nickname, and only you can hand out access.

Where does your voice go during a virtual meetup?

In all three platforms your voice leaves your device as a WebRTC or similar real-time stream and passes through a server before it reaches the others in the room. That server is the part that decides your privacy. In Hubs it is Dialog, a selective forwarding unit built on mediasoup. It receives each speaker's audio and forwards it to listeners, and it does not mix or store it. The stream is encrypted between your browser and Dialog with DTLS-SRTP, but this is not end-to-end encryption: whoever operates Dialog could in principle access the audio. On a self-hosted server, that operator is you.

Question Self-hosted Hubs VRChat and Horizon Worlds
Who operates the voice relay You, on the server you chose The platform company or its infrastructure providers
End-to-end encrypted No, encrypted in transit to the relay No, the platform's servers handle the audio
Recorded by default No, Dialog forwards and does not record Horizon Worlds keeps a rolling safety recording that can be sent to Meta when someone files a report
Where the relay sits Wherever your server lives Wherever the company runs it
Fallback relay Your own TURN server, if you configure one Managed by the platform

The location of the server decides which jurisdiction and which network can see your traffic metadata, even if nobody listens to the audio. A self-managed VPS puts it in a data centre you picked, a home server keeps it on your own connection, and a managed personal cloud such as Yundera keeps it on a server dedicated to you. In every case Dialog needs UDP ports reachable for media, so check that the setup you choose actually supports real-time voice before you invite people.

Account and identity data compared across Hubs, VRChat and Horizon Worlds

Voice is only part of the picture. An account also holds a profile that persists between sessions and can be linked to other services. The three platforms collect very different amounts.

  • Self-hosted Hubs, guest: a display name and the avatar picked for that session. There is no email, no birthdate and no persistent profile, so the only lasting trace is whatever your server logs, such as IP addresses in the web server logs.
  • Self-hosted Hubs, signed-in user: an email address stored in the server's PostgreSQL database, plus the rooms, scenes and avatars that user owns. No password is kept because sign-in uses emailed links. Deleting an account is an admin task you control.
  • VRChat: a username, an email address and a birthdate at sign-up, with the option of logging in through Steam or Meta. Some adult-only features need age verification through a third-party identity provider, so a government ID can enter the chain if a user opts in.
  • Horizon Worlds: a Meta account with a Meta Horizon profile. Children aged 10 to 12 need an account managed by a parent. A Meta account can be linked to Facebook or Instagram through Meta's Accounts Center, so meetup activity can sit next to the rest of your Meta identity.
  • Friends and social graph: VRChat and Horizon Worlds keep friends lists, presence and "who was where" data on their servers. Hubs has no friends list, so there is no social graph to collect.

For a family or small group the practical difference is this: on the commercial platforms every participant, including grandparents and children, creates and keeps a profile with a company. On your own Hubs server, most guests never create anything at all.

What can a social VR platform track about you beyond voice?

In a 3D room, your body becomes data. A headset reports where your head and hands are many times per second, and every social VR platform must send that movement to the others in the room. Researchers at UC Berkeley showed in 2023 that motion data alone could pick out one user from more than 50,000 with about 94% accuracy from 100 seconds of head and hand movement. So the question is not whether movement is collected but who keeps it.

  • Head and hand motion: Hubs relays positions through its Reticulum server to the other people in the room so avatars can move, and does not keep them after the session. On VRChat and Horizon Worlds the same stream passes through company servers, under their privacy policies.
  • Eye and face tracking: headsets such as the Meta Quest Pro can track gaze and facial expressions. Hubs in a browser does not use them. On Meta's platform these features depend on settings that users must check one by one.
  • Device and browser details: any web server sees a user agent string, screen size and IP address. On your Hubs server these sit in logs you can rotate or turn off.
  • Session history: Hubs keeps no presence list of who visited which room. Commercial platforms track presence to power friends lists and recommendations.
  • The headset's own operating system: a Quest collects device telemetry for Meta whatever app you run. Self-hosting Hubs does not remove that layer. Joining from a laptop browser does.

Self-hosting decides who holds the room data. It does not control the hardware your guests bring.

Is Hubs a safe choice for children and family gatherings?

For a closed family room, yes, and in some ways safer than the big platforms. Most risks children face in social VR come from strangers and open content catalogues, and a private Hubs server has neither. Some risks remain, though, and they now sit with you rather than a trust and safety team.

  • No stranger discovery: Hubs has no public world browser, friends requests or matchmaking. A child can only reach a room someone sent them a link to, which removes the main way strangers make contact on VRChat or Horizon Worlds.
  • No commerce or ads: there are no in-world purchases, currencies, subscriptions or advertising in Hubs. Nothing pushes a child to spend money or shares their behaviour with advertisers.
  • Less personal data to give away: since guests can join without an account, a child never has to enter an email or birthdate. That keeps you clear of the questions about parental consent raised by laws such as COPPA in the US, which covers under-13s, and GDPR Article 8 in the EU, where national thresholds range from 13 to 16.
  • Open media is the real weak spot: anyone in a room can paste a link to an image, video or 3D model unless the room owner turns that off. On a family room, restrict media sharing to the people who host.
  • Link leaks: a forwarded room URL is a key. Use invite-only rooms for children and change the link if it travels outside the family.
  • You are the moderator: Hubs has no 24/7 safety team and no report queue. An adult with owner rights should be present whenever children are in the room.

The safest pattern is simple: younger children join from a parent's laptop rather than their own headset, in a room an adult opened and stays in.

Room permissions and moderation tools for small private groups

Hubs gives room owners a short set of practical controls. They are built for a host who knows everyone in the room, not for policing thousands of strangers, which is exactly what a family or club needs.

  • Owner and moderator roles: the person who creates a room owns it and can promote other signed-in users to moderator. Moderators can mute and remove people, so one trusted adult or co-host can step in if the owner is busy presenting.
  • Member permissions: in room settings the owner decides what ordinary members may do, such as sharing media, drawing with the pen, spawning cameras, pinning objects or flying. Turn most of these off for a class and leave them on for a relaxed family evening.
  • Room size cap: standard deployments limit a room to 24 occupants by default, and the server admin can adjust the cap. A lower number stops a leaked link from turning a quiet meetup into a crowd.
  • Mute, remove and block: moderators can mute a microphone or remove a person from the room. Any user can also block someone, which hides their avatar and audio for that user only.
  • Lobby view: visitors can see the room from the lobby before they enter. The host can check who is waiting before they appear in the space.
  • Server-level controls: the admin panel lets whoever runs the server limit room creation and manage accounts. That is the layer where you stop someone abusing your server, not just a room.

What Hubs lacks is any automated moderation: no filters, no AI voice monitoring, no report queue reviewed by staff. Commercial platforms have those because their rooms are open to the public. In a private room the controls above, plus an adult present, are enough.

Which headsets, laptops and phones can join a Hubs room?

Because Hubs runs in a browser, the device question is really a browser question. Anything with a current browser can join in 2D, and devices whose browser supports WebXR can switch into immersive VR. Nobody has to install an app from an app store.

Device How it joins What to expect
Windows, macOS or Linux laptop Chrome, Edge, Firefox or Safari Full 2D experience with keyboard and mouse. The easiest option for grandparents and first-timers
Meta Quest 2, 3 or Pro Meta Quest Browser, using WebXR Full VR with hand controllers, but the headset's own Meta telemetry still applies
Other standalone headsets such as Pico Their built-in browser, if it supports WebXR Usually works in VR. Test before the event because browser support varies
PC VR headset through SteamVR A Chromium browser on the PC with WebXR enabled Full VR, with rendering on the PC's graphics card
Apple Vision Pro Safari on visionOS 2 or later, which supports WebXR Immersive mode is possible, with a different input model than controllers
iPhone or iPad Safari 2D only, touch controls. Fine for listening and chatting
Android phone or tablet Chrome 2D with touch controls. Older or low-end phones may struggle with detailed scenes

Two practical limits matter more than the brand. First, every device needs microphone permission granted in the browser, which trips up most first-time guests. Second, scene complexity sets the real hardware floor. A heavy scene with large textures that runs smoothly on a laptop can stutter on a three-year-old phone. Keep family rooms light, and mixed groups of headsets, laptops and phones can share the same space without issues.

What does self-hosting Hubs involve if you are not a sysadmin?

Hubs is not a one-container app. Community Edition deploys a set of services (web client, Reticulum, Dialog, Spoke, PostgreSQL, a TURN server and a reverse proxy) onto Kubernetes. If you do it by hand, expect a weekend, not an evening, and these concrete steps:

  • A domain and subdomains: Community Edition expects a root domain plus assets, stream and cors subdomains, each pointing at your server and each needing a valid TLS certificate.
  • A configuration file: you fill in input-values.yaml with your domain, admin email and secrets, run the supplied render_hcce.sh script to generate hcce.yaml, then apply it with kubectl apply -f hcce.yaml.
  • Open ports: besides TCP 80 and 443, the voice and relay services need TCP 4443 and 5349 plus a large UDP range (35000 to 60000 in the default configuration). Many home routers and some NAS setups make this the hardest step.
  • An email sender: sign-in links and admin login go out by email, so you need SMTP credentials from a mail provider. Without them, even you cannot sign in as admin.
  • A Kubernetes environment: a single-node distribution such as k3s is enough for a small group, but you still need to know where pods, logs and volumes live when something breaks.
  • Ongoing updates: you pull new images, re-render the config and redeploy, and back up the database first.

The less you want to touch, the more the hosting choice matters. A self-managed VPS gives you every knob and every chore. A home server or a capable NAS keeps hardware in your hands but leaves port forwarding to you. On a managed personal cloud such as Yundera, apps get a public HTTPS subdomain through NSL.SH mesh routing, so static IPs, port forwarding and certificates are handled. Whether Hubs's UDP media path is supported there is something to confirm before you commit.

How much does a private Hubs server cost for a small group over 3 years?

There is no licence fee, so the cost is infrastructure plus your time. VRChat and Horizon Worlds are free to join and pay for themselves through subscriptions, in-world sales and, for Meta, the wider business around your account. A private Hubs server swaps that model for bills you can see. Exact prices depend on the provider, so here is the shape of the cost over 36 months.

Cost component What drives it Over 3 years
Server compute Several always-on services, Kubernetes overhead and PostgreSQL 36 monthly bills on a VPS or managed host, or a one-off hardware purchase plus electricity at home
Bandwidth Dialog forwards every speaker to every listener: 10 people means up to 90 streams, 24 people up to 552 Flat if your plan includes generous traffic, a real line item if you pay per GB
Domain name One root domain, with subdomains included 3 yearly renewals
Email sending Magic-link sign-ins and admin login Often free at family volumes, a small monthly fee with some providers
Your time Initial setup, updates, backups and fixing broken rooms The largest cost for a non-sysadmin, front-loaded in year one

The bandwidth row is why hosting location matters. A home server costs little per month, but residential upload speeds cap how many people can talk at once. A self-managed VPS or a NAS sits at either end of the time-versus-control tradeoff, and a managed Personal Cloud Server such as Yundera moves setup work off your plate while the data stays on a server dedicated to you. For a group meeting once a week, compute and time dominate. Bandwidth only matters at the high end of the occupancy cap.

The central tradeoff: with Hubs you exchange the content, polish and scale of commercial social VR for control over who sees your voices, faces and identities.
